content_voiceover: This slide introduces inhibitors to clotting factor as a chapter topic. Inhibitors are IgG alloantibodies that develop against exogenous, infused factor eight or factor nine, neutralizing the therapeutic effect of clotting factor concentrates. They represent one of the most serious complications in modern hemophilia treatment, because they render standard factor replacement ineffective. Patients with inhibitors carry a substantially higher disease burden, with more severe bleeding episodes, more complications, more hospitalizations, and higher mortality compared to inhibitor-negative patients. Inhibitors are far more common in hemophilia A than hemophilia B, developing in roughly thirty percent of patients with severe hemophilia A, compared to five percent or less in severe hemophilia B, a ratio worth remembering for boards. Potential risk factors for inhibitor development include race, family history, genotype and immune regulatory genes, hemophilia severity, and the intensity and type of factor replacement used, themes that are explored in more detail in subsequent slides.
